discovery: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computation, including topological codes
motivation: Quantum states were once thought too fragile to protect: measurement destroys them, and the no-cloning theorem rules out simple redundancy. Shor (1995) and Steane (1996) showed that this is not so. By encoding a logical qubit non-locally in entangled states of many physical qubits, errors can be detected and undone without learning the encoded information. Kitaev's toric code (1997) turned this into physics: information protected by topological order, with an accuracy threshold for fault tolerance. These ideas created the field of fault-tolerant quantum computation, and recent experiments with superconducting and atomic platforms have run surface-code memories below threshold, so that logical errors fall as codes grow. Their reach goes well beyond computing. Topological codes changed how condensed-matter physicists think about quantum phases, and quantum error correction now underlies our understanding of how holographic spacetime emerges from boundary entanglement. It is a deep, unifying principle of quantum physics.
